title: belie / belittle / betray
core: Three verbs that start with *be-* and blur together on the page, though only two of them actually compete for meaning. Those two sit at opposite ends of one axis: whether a surface hides an inner truth or leaks it. The third has nothing to do with concealment at all — it's about assigning worth — and gets chosen on shape alone by test-takers who register the prefix and stop reading.

words.nuance: **Belie**'s subject is the cover story — the composed face, the tidy façade, the reassuring number — and what follows is the truth being masked or knocked down. It is the only one of the three that runs concealment-ward; it never means "reveal," no matter how clearly the sentence lets you infer the hidden truth.

**Belittle** is the outlier: no hidden truth, no leak, just a speaker sizing something down. It requires a human agent talking *about* something from a position of assumed height, and its tone is calm dismissal — "anyone could have done that" — not the involuntary self-exposure the other two describe.

**Betray** runs the opposite direction from *belie*: its subject is the traitorous detail — a tremor, a flush, a half-second pause — and what follows is the secret getting out. The leak is always unintentional, which is why the word carries a faint taste of defection even when nobody has done anything wrong.

exam_note: Watch the subject of the verb: *her steady voice* belies panic, *her shaking hands* betray it — swap them and the sentence still parses but points the wrong way, which is exactly the trap.
